newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumers still spending freely in January.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumers still spending freely in January.

text.p: U.S. consumers continued to spend their money at a brisk pace in January, a trend which will provide a solid foundation for growth in the overall economy for the rest of the first quarter, economists said.
A report on Monday showed personal consumption rose 0.7 percent in January, slightly exceeding the 0.6-percent consensus forecast of a Reuters poll of economists.
Personal income rose 0.3 percent, topping the forecast for a 0.1-percent gain.
"We're seeing good strength in the new year. Basically the consumer is in good shape and has good income support," said Alan Levenson, money market economist at UBS Securities.
While the continuing growth in consumption will likely bring cheer to American businesses, it could trouble Federal Reserve policymakers, analysts said.
Many economists expect the Fed to raise official short-term interest rates in coming months if the economy does not slow from its rapid pace of the fourth quarter.
Real gross domestic product grew 3.9 percent in the fourth quarter, a rate seen almost sure to boost inflation over time.
"This data may not show it, but we are in the process of slowing from the fourth quarter," said Mitchell Held, chief economist at Smith Barney Inc.

"That's healthy, because we expect the economy to grow closer to its (maximum noninflationary) growth rate of about 2.5 percent and we'd rather see it do that on its own than through Fed actions," Held added.

Consumption may get a boost over the next couple months from faster tax returns resulting from the rise in electronic filing, Held said. Through February 21, returns were running 19 percent higher than at the same time a year ago, he said.
"Last year they caught up in April and May, and I think they'll catch up again. But once that money comes into consumers' hands, they spend it and they spend it quickly," Held said.
Other economists agreed that the pace of spending would slow in coming months, citing likely peaks in spending on autos, durable goods and services.
"This report puts the consumer on a relatively buoyant trajectory into the first quarter, however parts of the report look a little odd," said Bruce Steinberg, economist at Merrill Lynch.
"Services spending has been strong for several months. That's not typical and I suspect it's unlikely to be sustained. The rest of the spending in the report looks less impressive," Steinberg added.

But the Fed probably will look past the income and spending data to Friday's release on February employment conditions as it sizes up the health of the consumer and the economy as a whole, Steinberg said.
With the unemployment rate hovering below 5.5 percent and the economy seen adding over 200,000 new jobs in February, the Fed may opt to tighten credit soon, analysts said.

"The Fed is not paying as much attention to this (income/spending) report as it is to the employment numbers," said Steinberg. "I think the Fed can wait (to tighten), but whether or not they do depends on how the next several employment reports go."
